title: Draupadi
hook: the man who killed her sons in their sleep is dragged before her in ropes, and in the Bhagavata's telling she asks for him to be set free

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi and the empty pot: Krishna arrived hungry and made a meal of one leaf on the rim.

Ropes around his arms, Ashvatthama is pushed forward and made to stand in front of her. He is the son of Drona, the Pandavas' own teacher. On the last night of the war he crept into their sleeping camp and killed Draupadi's sons. Arjuna has caught him and tied him up like an animal. Krishna has told Arjuna he may kill him. Instead, Arjuna brings him to the mother of the dead. Last year on this path, the Mahabharata's telling of this moment ended with a jewel. Today the Bhagavata Purana tells it, and she says something else.
screen: `THE KILLER, IN ROPES.` → `BROUGHT TO THE MOTHER.` → `THE BHAGAVATA TELLS IT.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana's first book, Draupadi sees the son of her husbands' teacher bound and ashamed, and she bows to him. Then she speaks, in paraphrase. Let him go. Let him go. He is the son of the teacher from whom you learned your bows and your weapons. In him, the teacher is still here. Then the line the whole scene turns on: his mother, Kripi, is still alive. Don't let her weep the way I am weeping now. The text calls her words fair, kind and full of dharma, and some of those present agree. Bhima does not. This man killed sleeping children, he says, and deserves to die. Krishna finds a way through. Arjuna cuts the jewel from Ashvatthama's head and shaves his hair, a punishment the text treats as a kind of death for one like him, and sends him out of the camp alive. Set the two tellings side by side, without ranking them. In the Mahabharata, Draupadi refuses food until she sees the jewel taken from his head. In the Bhagavata, she asks for his life. Readers have held both. Her grief doesn't vanish; she names it, I am weeping. Her mercy doesn't excuse him; the punishment still falls. And the reason she gives is another mother. She doesn't ask what he deserves. She asks who else will be sitting where she is sitting tonight.
screen: `SHE BOWS TO THE BOUND MAN` · `HE IS OUR TEACHER'S SON` · `LET HIS MOTHER NOT WEEP AS I DO` · `TWO TELLINGS, BOTH HELD`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who hurt you, small or large; you don't have to forgive them in this sit, and Draupadi's mercy doesn't erase the harm. Just look past the person, once, to someone who loves them, a mother, a child, a friend, and let that person be there for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold that other person in prayer. If the hurt is still happening, or grief is too much, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
Draupadi. In the Bhagavata, with her sons' killer in ropes before her, she asks for his life so that his mother won't weep as she does. Today's word.
Your line: Draupadi. Mercy, so that another mother would not have to weep. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus who read or hear the Bhagavata Purana meet this scene early in its first book, sometimes in long public recitations, and storytellers set it beside the Mahabharata's own telling.

myth: in the Bhagavata, Draupadi demands Ashvatthama's death
in the Bhagavata she asks for his life; in the Mahabharata she asks for the jewel from his head.
Draupadi's reason is that his mother should not weep as she does
she names Kripi, and her own weeping.
Ashvatthama walks free with no punishment at all
his jewel is cut away and his hair shaved, and he is sent out of the camp.

fork.setup: you're Draupadi. the man who killed your sons stands bound before you, and your husband waits for your word. what do you say?
options: let him go; his mother still lives.
fork.reveal: in the Bhagavata she bows to him and asks for his release, so that Kripi won't weep as she does. the punishment still falls, but he lives.

chat.says: Why would Draupadi ask them to spare the man who killed her sons?
options: In the Bhagavata, so his mother, Kripi, won't weep the way she is weeping.
In the Bhagavata, because she had stopped grieving and felt nothing now.
In the Bhagavata, because she thought he had done nothing wrong.
chat.meaning: In Bhagavata 1.7 Draupadi names her grief and asks mercy because Ashvatthama's mother, Kripi, still lives; the punishment still falls.

Ashvatthama.meaning: Drona's son, who killed Draupadi's sons in their sleep

Drona.meaning: the Pandavas' teacher of arms, Ashvatthama's father

Kripi.meaning: Ashvatthama's mother, for whose sake Draupadi asks mercy

Bhagavata Purana.meaning: a devotional retelling of Krishna's story

Bhima.meaning: the strongest Pandava, who wants Ashvatthama dead
